name: Times Literary Supplement cryptic crossword No 1,156

solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing; the grid proves the blog's enumeration wrong at 19 across, recounted from the answer here

clue.text: “To miss the march of this retreating world Into vain — that are not walled” (Wilfred Owen)

definitions.text: “To miss the march of this retreating world Into vain — that are not walled” (Wilfred Owen)

blocks.clueFragment: “To miss the march of this retreating world Into vain — that are not walled”
blocks.note: surface reading: lines of verse about withdrawing from the world into empty strongholds, with a gap
setter's reading: the source names the First World War poet, whose poem Strange Meeting supplies the missing word

explanation.walkthrough: This is a quotation clue: the line comes from Owen's Strange Meeting, where the dead soldier imagines retreating into proud fortresses that have no walls.
explanation.definitionFit: Fortresses guarding a town fit a poem steeped in warfare, and the paradox of unwalled strongholds is the point.

clue.text: “The game — clipp’d and arm’d for fight Does the Rising Sun affright.” (William Blake)

definitions.text: “The game — clipp’d and arm’d for fight Does the Rising Sun affright.” (William Blake)

blocks.clueFragment: “The game — clipp’d and arm’d for fight Does the Rising Sun affright.”
blocks.note: surface reading: verse about a creature trimmed and spurred for combat, with a gap
setter's reading: the source names the poet whose Auguries of Innocence holds the line

explanation.walkthrough: This is a quotation clue from Blake's Auguries of Innocence; a game bird bred for cockfighting had its comb clipped and metal spurs fitted.
explanation.definitionFit: A fighting rooster is the bird that crows at dawn, so its cruel use frightens even the rising sun.

clue.text: Record set on a river by an all-male coxed pair?

definitions.text: Record set on a river by an all-male coxed pair?

blocks.note: surface reading: a best-ever time achieved in a rowing race; setter's reading: a written account of a journey along the Thames
setter's reading: two male rowers plus a male cox make a trio of men sharing one craft

explanation.surface: A rowing crew of two men with a cox breaks a river speed record.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Record' is a book here, not a sporting best: Jerome K. Jerome's comic novel records a boating holiday on the Thames.
explanation.definitionFit: Jerome's 1889 comic travelogue follows a trio of friends rowing up the Thames, so it is literally their river record.

clue.text: .Booker-winner‘s note on archbishop’s address in Bow

indicators.note: Bow is in London's East End, and Cockney speech there drops the aitch at the start of words

blocks.note: D is a note of the musical scale
an archbishop is styled His Grace

explanation.surface: A prize-winning novelist's note is placed on an archbishop's speech delivered in East London.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Address' is the form of title, not a speech. Bow is a Cockney district, and Cockneys drop their aitches; in a down clue 'on' puts the note on top.
explanation.definitionFit: J. M. Coetzee's novel won the Booker Prize in 1999, so the book title is named by its award.

clue.text: Erica Jong’s fear? Losing an edge for storytelling

indicators.note: an edge of a word is one of its ends, and losing it means the opening letter falls away

blocks.note: Erica Jong's best-known novel is Fear of Flying

explanation.surface: A novelist's anxiety leaves her blunted when it comes to telling stories.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that 'fear' points to the title Fear of Flying; the front F goes.
explanation.definitionFit: Telling stories is a familiar euphemism for telling untruths, so storytelling here means fibbing.

clue.text: Endless success, having opened tremendous O’Neill play

indicators.note: without an end means the final letter is cut and only the rest is kept
something that has opened another thing has gone inside it, sitting within its walls

blocks.note: a hit is a success; the last letter is dropped
huge is a synonym for tremendous

explanation.surface: A huge stage hit that just keeps running, after opening big, for an O'Neill drama.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Endless' trims only the last letter, not both ends; 'opened' looks like a premiere but means getting inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Hughie is a short one-act drama by Eugene O'Neill, a monologue set in a seedy New York hotel lobby.

clue.text: A little drink with posh Penny – result!

blocks.note: U means upper-class, as in U and non-U speech
p is the abbreviation for a penny
a shot is a small measure of spirits

explanation.surface: Someone shares a small tipple with a well-to-do woman called Penny and celebrates a success.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Penny' looks like a woman's name but is just the coin's abbreviation, and 'posh' is the crossword U.
explanation.definitionFit: The final outcome of a process is its eventual consequence, a standard synonym pair.

clue.text: Potter’s associate sculpting no meagre herring

indicators.note: a sculptor works raw material into a new form, so these letters are moulded into a fresh shape

blocks.note: the letters as written

explanation.surface: A potter's colleague is carving a generously sized fish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Potter' reads as a ceramicist beside a sculptor, but it is Harry Potter.
explanation.definitionFit: She is Harry's clever best friend and companion throughout J. K. Rowling's wizarding novels.

clue.text: Why a Dr. gets mixed up in murderous deed?

definitions.text: Why a Dr. gets mixed up in murderous deed?

indicators.note: things mixed up are jumbled out of their proper order, so the letters get rearranged

blocks.note: the letters as written
the letters as written

explanation.surface: Someone asks why a doctor became entangled in a killing.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is also the definition: Dr Jekyll gets mixed up in murder because his other self commits it. 'Murderous' colours the deed without supplying letters.
explanation.definitionFit: In Stevenson's novella the doctor's evil alter ego tramples a child and kills Sir Danvers Carew.

clue.text: Bassanio’s man gets stood up in house party

indicators.note: in a down clue, going up means reading from bottom to top, the wrong way round
one thing placed in another sits inside it, enclosed on both sides

blocks.note: to stand for office is to run for it
Leo is one of the twelve astrological houses
a do is a party or celebration

explanation.surface: A nobleman's servant is jilted at a house party.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stood up' looks like being jilted, but it is RAN, turned upward. 'House' is a zodiac sign, not a building.
explanation.definitionFit: Leonardo is Bassanio's servant in Shakespeare's The Merchant of Venice, a minor attendant role.

clue.text: Dame involved in crime withholding number a car possessed

indicators.note: to withhold something is to keep it held back inside, so one piece is kept within another

blocks.note: Dame Agatha Christie, the crime novelist
N is the abbreviation for number

explanation.surface: A crime writer keeps quiet about the number of a haunted car.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dame involved in crime' is the queen of detective fiction.
explanation.definitionFit: Stephen King's horror novel features a 1958 Plymouth Fury with a malevolent will of its own.

clue.text: After changing taps, what James might turn for Kate?

indicators.note: basin taps are marked for hot and cold, so swapping taps means trading one of those labels for the other

blocks.note: Henry James wrote The Turn of the Screw
H for hot replaces C for cold

explanation.surface: A plumber asks what fitting a man named James might turn for a woman named Kate.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark covers the title The Turn of the Screw; the C becomes H.
explanation.definitionFit: Katherina, called Kate, is the scolding heroine of Shakespeare's The Taming of the Shrew.

clue.text: The Foreign Legion has not use for my king

indicators.note: having no use for something means discarding it, so those letters are thrown out

blocks.note: le is French for the
a legion is a large army unit
taken as written, then removed

explanation.surface: A legionnaire's outfit has no use for the speaker's monarch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The Foreign Legion' reads as one unit but splits into a foreign 'the' and a legion.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's tragic monarch who divides his realm among his daughters, an obvious royal in a literary puzzle.

clue.text: Middle-Earth realm visited by porky boatman

indicators.note: a visitor goes inside the place visited, so one piece ends up within another

blocks.note: Gondor is a kingdom in Tolkien's Middle-earth
porky is short for pork pie, rhyming slang for lie

explanation.surface: A kingdom in Tolkien's world receives a visit from a rather plump ferryman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Porky' looks like it describes the boatman as fat, but it is rhyming slang: a porky (pork pie) is a lie.
explanation.definitionFit: The Venetian oarsman who propels a gondola standing at the stern is a specific kind of boatman.

clue.text: Hunger was his king, having escaped a US manhunt

definitions.note: a phrase meaning the author of Hunger, standing for a person's name

indicators.note: letters that have escaped have broken loose from their order and run off in a jumble

blocks.note: K is the chess abbreviation for king
the letters as written

explanation.surface: A starving monarch got away from an American pursuit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hunger was his' looks like a king's suffering, but it means the novel Hunger was his work.
explanation.definitionFit: The Norwegian Nobel laureate made his name with the 1890 novel Hunger, about a starving young writer in Oslo.

clue.text: Playwright who might shy away from Christmas

blocks.note: Noel is another word for Christmas
a coward is someone who shrinks from danger

explanation.surface: A dramatist who would rather avoid the festive season altogether.
explanation.walkthrough: The coward comes 'from Christmas' in the sense of following straight on from it.
explanation.definitionFit: The English dramatist wrote Private Lives and Blithe Spirit, witty drawing-room comedies of the twentieth century.

clue.text: Conflict about road award for a gateway to Lewis

indicators.note: brought about means turned round, so this piece faces the other way

blocks.note: war is armed conflict
Rd is the abbreviation for road
the OBE is a British honour, Officer of the Order of the British Empire

explanation.surface: A dispute over a road-safety prize given for an entrance to a Scottish island.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lewis' suggests the Hebridean island, but it is C. S. Lewis.
explanation.definitionFit: In The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe the children reach Narnia through a cupboard of fur coats.

clue.text: Creep lawyer from Maycomb initially ignored

indicators.note: ignoring what comes initially means passing over the opening letter and keeping the rest

blocks.note: Atticus Finch is the lawyer in Maycomb, Alabama, in To Kill a Mockingbird

explanation.surface: A sleazy small-town attorney is snubbed from the start.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Creep' looks like a noun for a nasty person, but it is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To move forward slowly, a tiny distance at a time, is to edge or crawl along.

clue.text: A schoolboy error finally breaks grave individual

indicators.note: at the very end, so only the closing letter of the word is taken
something that breaks into a whole splits it open and sits in the gap

blocks.note: a tomb is a grave
the final letter
own means individual, belonging to oneself

explanation.surface: A pupil's mistake ends up ruining a serious person.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Grave individual' reads as a solemn person but splits into two separate words, with the error's last letter wedged between them.
explanation.definitionFit: Thomas Hughes's Tom Brown's School Days made its hero the archetypal Victorian public schoolboy at Rugby.

clue.text: Briefly imagine a way to describe Clyde Wynant?

definitions.text: a way to describe Clyde Wynant

indicators.note: said briefly means cut short, so the final letter is lopped off

blocks.note: to imagine is to think

explanation.surface: Someone is invited to sum up a character in a few words.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the indirect definition through a novel's title.
explanation.definitionFit: Clyde Wynant is the missing inventor in Dashiell Hammett's The Thin Man, the gaunt figure of the title.

clue.text: A word for go astray in a Nigerian novel

indicators.note: letters gone astray have wandered from their places, so their order is jumbled

blocks.note: the letters as written

explanation.surface: A reader looks for a synonym of 'err' in an African book.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A word for go astray' reads like a request for a synonym such as err; the words themselves are the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Chinua Achebe's 1964 novel, the third of his African Trilogy, centres on an Igbo chief priest.

clue.text: Perhaps Jane worried about American close to Tarzan

definitions.note: Jane is one bearer of the surname

indicators.note: to be about something is to go round it, enclosing it
the close of a word is its end, so only its last letter is used

blocks.note: ate, as in ate at, means worried or troubled
US is the abbreviation for American
the final letter

explanation.surface: Jane frets about an American getting close to Tarzan, the Jane of the jungle.
explanation.walkthrough: Tarzan's Jane is the obvious one, but the definition wants a surname that Jane is 'perhaps' paired with.
explanation.definitionFit: The novelist of Pride and Prejudice is the most famous Jane in literature, so the surname completes the name.

clue.text: Some assure us a harpy recalled Xerxes by another name

indicators.note: some of a phrase is only part of it, so the letters lie within
called back means brought back the way it came, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: a run of letters spanning these words

explanation.surface: Some people reassure us that a shrewish woman once recalled the Persian king.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters read right to left across 'assure us a harpy'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Book of Esther calls the Persian king Ahasuerus, generally identified with Xerxes I.

clue.text: Soldier that’s run into the Oracle of Delphi?

indicators.note: something put into another goes inside it

blocks.note: R is the cricket abbreviation for run
an oracle is a wise counsellor, a sage, and the question mark marks it as an example

explanation.surface: A soldier dashes headlong into the ancient Greek shrine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Run into' looks like a meeting, but run is R and into puts it inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Sarge is the informal address for a sergeant, a non-commissioned army rank.

clue.text: Live rail cut in half around Paddington?

indicators.note: halving cuts a word down to two of its four letters, losing the back half
turned around means facing the other way

blocks.note: to be is to live or exist
the word as written

explanation.surface: A live rail is cut near Paddington, the London station.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Live rail' and 'Paddington' suggest the London rail terminus; Paddington is the bear from Peru.
explanation.definitionFit: Michael Bond's marmalade-loving character from darkest Peru is an example of the animal, hence the question mark.

clue.text: Look after little sailor in Harry Hole’s patch

blocks.note: OS stands for ordinary seaman, a junior sailor
lo is an old word meaning look

explanation.surface: Someone takes care of a small seaman on a detective's beat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Look after' looks like caring for someone; in a down clue 'after' just means placed below.
explanation.definitionFit: Jo Nesbø's detective Harry Hole works for the police in the Norwegian capital, his home territory.

clue.text: One behind Heart of Midlothian? That’s too much!

blocks.note: sc. is short for scilicet, Latin for that is to say
OTT is over the top, meaning excessive

explanation.surface: A football fan stands behind Hearts and complains it is all too much.
explanation.walkthrough: Heart of Midlothian is also an Edinburgh football club, so 'One behind' reads as a supporter. It is the novel, and the one behind it is its author.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Walter Scott wrote The Heart of Midlothian in 1818, so he is the person responsible for that book.

clue.text: Junkie writer with digs underground, they say

indicators.note: what people say is spoken, so the sound counts rather than the spelling

blocks.note: burrows are holes dug by animals as homes

explanation.surface: A drug-addicted author lives in a basement flat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Digs' is British slang for lodgings, which suits the surface; here they are an animal's underground holes.
explanation.definitionFit: William S. Burroughs's first novel was Junkie (1953), about his heroin addiction, so he is its author.

clue.text: Taking down zip to set husband free?

indicators.note: setting someone free lets them go, so that letter leaves the word

blocks.note: zip is slang for nothing
h is the abbreviation for husband

explanation.surface: Undoing a zip to release a trapped husband.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Taking down' and 'zip' suggest undressing, but taking down is writing a note.
explanation.definitionFit: To take down words is to write them, recording or jotting them as notes.

clue.text: Officer who saw a former Danish king develop rare bond

definitions.text: Officer who saw a former Danish king

indicators.note: to develop is to grow into a new form, so the letters change shape

blocks.note: the letters as written

explanation.surface: A soldier who glimpsed a dead Danish monarch forms an unusual friendship.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'former Danish king' is the ghost of Hamlet's father.
explanation.definitionFit: Bernardo is one of the sentries on the battlements at Elsinore who sees the ghost in Hamlet's opening scene.
